# session-control

[![CI](https://github.com/casonk/session-control/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/casonk/session-control/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)](LICENSE) [![Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue)](pyproject.toml) [![Coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/casonk/session-control/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/casonk/session-control)

Private web control plane for local AI assistant session files.

`session-control` scans local Codex, Claude Code, Continue, GitHub Copilot CLI,
Grok Build, and Google Antigravity CLI (AGY) session stores, summarizes what
each session was about, shows the command to resume it, and moves old sessions
into a local trash directory from a small Flask web UI.

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.10 or newer
- Flask, installed through the package metadata
- Local session files from one or more supported tools:
  - Codex: `~/.codex/sessions`
  - Claude Code: `~/.claude/projects`
  - Continue: `~/.continue/sessions`
  - GitHub Copilot CLI: `~/.copilot/session-state`
  - Grok Build: `~/.grok/sessions`
  - Google Antigravity CLI (AGY): `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli`

## Quick Start

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
session-control scan
session-control web
```

The web UI binds to `127.0.0.1:5420` by default. For phone access, keep the app
on loopback and expose it through a trusted local proxy such as
`wiring-harness` Caddy with mTLS or a WireGuard-only route.

## claude.ai chats

Chats made in the claude.ai web app are not on disk. For Claude Enterprise organizations,
Anthropic's Compliance API serves them, so `session-control sync-web` copies them into a local
cache that the scan lists as provider `claude-web`.

1. A primary owner enables the Compliance API at claude.ai, Organization settings, API.
2. Create a key there with the `read:compliance_user_data` scope. An Admin API key from the
   Console does not work (403).
3. Put the key in `SESSION_CONTROL_ANTHROPIC_COMPLIANCE_KEY_FILE` (an owner-only file) or
   `SESSION_CONTROL_ANTHROPIC_COMPLIANCE_KEY`. Set `SESSION_CONTROL_ANTHROPIC_USER_EMAIL` to
   your address if the key can see other people's chats.
4. Run `session-control sync-web` (add `--full` to re-read everything). Later runs fetch only
   chats updated since the last one, and chats you delete in claude.ai leave the cache.

Each chat is stored as one owner-only JSON file with its text messages (tool calls and results
are left out). Titles and previews are redacted like every other provider. "Resume" is an
`xdg-open` of the chat's claude.ai address, and deleting a session here removes only the local
copy; the next sync fetches it again. Personal claude.ai accounts have no such API, only the
Settings, Privacy, Export data download. ChatGPT is not covered yet; OpenAI's Compliance API
is Enterprise-only and its endpoints have not been confirmed.

## Configuration

Copy `config/session-control.env.example` to
`config/session-control.env.local` and adjust local paths or proxy origins.
The `.local` file is gitignored.

Common variables:

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `SESSION_CONTROL_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | Flask bind host |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_PORT` | `5420` | Flask bind port |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` | unset | External origin used by a trusted proxy |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` | unset | Comma-separated extra origins for CSRF checks |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_GROK_ROOT` | `~/.grok` | Grok Build state root |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_AGY_ROOT` | `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli` | Google Antigravity CLI state root |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_WEBCHAT_DIR` | `~/.local/share/session-control/webchats` | Owner-only cache of claude.ai chats |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_ANTHROPIC_COMPLIANCE_KEY` | unset | Compliance Access Key (or `..._KEY_FILE` for a file holding it) |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_ANTHROPIC_USER_EMAIL` | unset | Keep only this user's chats when the key sees the whole organization |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_TRASH_DIR` | `~/.local/share/session-control/trash` | Delete destination |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_DIGEST_DIR` | `~/.local/share/session-control/digests` | Private category/repo termination records |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS` | `7` | Days to keep restorable raw files |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_DIGEST_RETENTION_DAYS` | `365` | Days to keep condensed records |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_PRUNE_OLDER_THAN` | `180d` | Default age for scheduled pruning |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_PRUNE_SHORT_SUBAGENT_PERCENT` | unset | Short subagent age as a share of scheduled age, such as `25%` |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_CREW_CHIEF_REGISTRY` | `~/.local/state/crew-chief/code-sessions.jsonl` | Sessions launched by `crew-chief code`, labelled `local · <model>` |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_PRUNE_SHORT_SUBAGENT_MULTIPLIER` | unset | Short subagents pruned this many times sooner, such as `4x`; use instead of percentage |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_MONITOR_WEBTERM_CLIENT_CERT` | unset | Dedicated client certificate for the WebTerm HTTPS probe |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_MONITOR_WEBTERM_CLIENT_KEY` | unset | Matching private key for the WebTerm probe certificate |
| `SESSION_CONTROL_MONITOR_WEBTERM_CA_CERT` | unset | Additional CA certificate used to verify WebTerm's server certificate |

Set `SESSION_CONTROL_ALLOW_REMOTE=1` only when intentionally binding the Flask
app outside loopback. The preferred phone path is still a loopback app behind
`wiring-harness`/Caddy or WireGuard.

## End a session from chat

When an agent is working under this repository's `AGENTS.md`, a clear command
such as “kill this session” tells it to run `session-control terminate-current`,
tell the user to manually close or delete the hosted chat, and end its turn.
The command requires Codex's `CODEX_THREAD_ID` environment
variable and matches exactly one local Codex session. It removes that session
from the provider store immediately by moving its files into restorable trash.
It cannot close the host chat thread or erase remote records. The user must
close or delete the chat in their chat client. If the provider
continues writing after the move, new local artifacts may appear; run rotation
or delete those again after the host thread stops.

Every normal delete, prune, self termination, and merge records a private,
metadata-only digest with category, repository basename, and counts. The
**Coverage** page shows category and repository totals only. Titles, previews,
transcripts, full paths, and session IDs are not kept in these records. The
daily prune run also expires valid trash entries after 7 days and digest records
after 365 days by default. Use `session-control rotate --dry-run` to preview
expiration or `session-control rotate` to run it immediately. Restoring an entry
within its trash retention window does not erase its termination record.

## Resume Commands

The scanner emits provider-specific resume commands:

- Codex: `codex resume <session-id>` or `codex resume --model <model> <session-id>` when the session records a model
- Claude Code: `claude --resume <session-id>`, or for sessions started with
  [`crew-chief code`](https://github.com/casonk/crew-chief) on a local model,
  `crew-chief --url <server> code --model <model> --backend <backend> -- --resume <session-id>`
  so the session reopens on the same local backend
- Continue: `cn --fork <session-id>`
- GitHub Copilot CLI: `copilot --resume=<session-id>`
- Grok Build: `grok --resume <session-id>`
- Google Antigravity CLI (AGY): `agy --conversation <session-id>`

When a session records a workspace, the command is prefixed with `cd <workspace>`.
Set `SESSION_CONTROL_CODEX_RESUME_MODEL` to force a known-good Codex model for
web-launched resumes when the global Codex default is not supported by the
machine's current auth mode.

## Continue in a different provider

A transcript can only be resumed by the provider that wrote it, so switching
provider is a handoff: session-control writes a context brief (title, workspace
and, for Codex and Claude Code sources, the recent conversation) under
`~/.local/share/session-control/handoffs/` and starts a **new** session in the
target provider (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Continue, Copilot or Antigravity)
that reads it first. Use "Continue in" on a session's page, or:

```bash
session-control handoff <public-id> --to claude   # prints the brief path and command
session-control handoff <public-id> --to codex --run
```

Treat the brief as a summary, not a transcript. Any provider can be a source or
a target; a session is not offered a handoff to its own provider (use the normal
resume).

## Shared agent memory

Removing a session would otherwise lose what it learned. Before delete, bulk delete,
`prune` or `terminate-current` moves files to trash, session-control writes a condensed,
redacted note to `~/.local/share/session-control/memory/` (private, `0700`/`0600`):

```text
memory/INDEX.md                      one line per note, newest first
memory/entries/<provider>-<id>.md    summary, opening request, outcome, files mentioned
```

Any assistant can read these files directly, or query them:

```bash
session-control memory search "caddy mtls"
session-control memory list
session-control memory show claude-<id>
session-control condense <session-id>      # write a note without removing the session
session-control condense --all             # backfill notes for existing sessions
session-control condense --all --older-than 30d --provider claude
session-control condense --all --refresh --model qwen3:14b   # upgrade notes with a local model
session-control condense --all --stale     # also refresh notes whose session changed
session-control memory failures            # notes whose model pass failed
session-control condense --failed          # redo only those
session-control memory prune --older-than 365d --dry-run
session-control memory prune --max-per-repo 50
session-control prune --no-condense        # opt out for one run
```

In the web UI, open **Memory** in the top bar to search and read notes (and delete one),
or use **Condense to memory** on a session page; sessions that have a note show a
"memory note" badge in the list.

The `skills/session-memory` skill tells agents when and how to search the memory; link it
into your assistants' skill directories (for example `ln -s "$PWD/skills/session-memory"
~/.claude/skills/session-memory`). To share it across agents, add a line to your agent instructions such as: "Before
starting related work, run `session-control memory search <topic>`; notes are summaries,
so verify against the repository."

The default condenser is deterministic and offline. For a model-written summary run a
local Ollama (for example the `crew-chief` service) and set
`SESSION_CONTROL_CONDENSER=ollama`, `SESSION_CONTROL_CONDENSER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434`
and `SESSION_CONTROL_CONDENSER_MODEL=<model>`. Session text is only ever sent to a loopback
host, and if the model is unreachable the extractive note is written instead. If a note
cannot be written, the removal is refused rather than losing the session; set
`SESSION_CONTROL_CONDENSE_ON_REMOVE=0` to disable. Notes are kept until you delete them (`memory prune` removes old or surplus ones).

In the web UI a model call never blocks a request: delete, bulk delete and **Condense to
memory** write the extractive note immediately, then a worker thread upgrades it with the
model. The CLI, prune timer and backfill run the model synchronously.

Install the daily backfill timer (04:05, `condense --all --stale`) with
`./scripts/install_condense_timer.sh`. The note view renders a small, escaped markdown
subset (headings, lists, bold, code); links and raw HTML are never rendered.

## Subagent sessions

The session list marks recognized subagents and provides a **Session origin**
filter. Detection uses Codex child-thread or agent-role metadata and Claude Code
sidechain metadata or `subagents/` storage. The label also appears in session
details and federated inventories. **Other sessions** includes sessions without
subagent evidence; provider files do not always reveal whether an agent started
a top-level CLI session.

**Short subagents** flags recognized subagents whose first and last recorded
events are at most five minutes apart. This is a cleanup review cue, not proof
that the process exited or that the work has no value. Use the filter and
**Select all visible** to review a batch before moving it to trash.

## Multiple machines

Session stores remain local to their owning machine. Do not synchronize raw
provider directories or transcripts. Instead, a node can export a deliberately
restricted inventory containing only a title, provider, timestamp, workspace
basename, size/count metadata, and model:

```bash
session-control inventory --json
session-control publish-inventory \
  --url https://session-control.example.internal/api/federation/v1/inventories/air \
  --token-file ~/.config/session-control/federation-air.token \
  --ca-file ~/.config/wiring-harness/certs/ca.crt \
  --cert-file ~/.config/wiring-harness/certs/client.crt \
  --key-file ~/.config/wiring-harness/certs/client.key
```

The central node enables `SESSION_CONTROL_FEDERATION_STORE_DIR` and assigns a
distinct owner-only token to each approved node in
`SESSION_CONTROL_FEDERATION_TOKENS`. Its **All machines** page displays local
and received inventories by host. Remote records are read-only: opening,
resuming, deleting, and restoring remain local operations. Put the receiver
behind the existing Caddy mTLS route; the per-node bearer token is an additional
authorization check, not a substitute for mTLS.

Codex itself can set permission defaults in `~/.codex/config.toml`, for example
`sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"`, or per
launch with `codex resume --sandbox ... --ask-for-approval ...`. For Codex
sessions, session-control shows the last recorded sandbox/approval policy and
adds a launch-time dropdown with these presets:

- `default`: rely on Codex config files
- `recorded`: reuse the session's last recorded sandbox and approval policy
- `read-only`: launch with `--sandbox read-only --ask-for-approval on-request`
- `auto`: launch with `--sandbox workspace-write --ask-for-approval on-request`
- `full-auto`: launch with `--sandbox danger-full-access --ask-for-approval never`

Set `SESSION_CONTROL_CODEX_PERMISSION_PRESET` to choose the default dropdown
selection for web-launched Codex resumes.

## Provider Format Diagnostics

Session Control probes the local formats it understands while scanning. If a
provider changes an index, session file, workspace file, or event log schema,
the index page shows a provider-specific warning without suppressing sessions
from other providers. The warning names only the local file or session
directory, never its full private path. Update the minimized fixtures and
scanner support before relying on a new format.

The Open action creates a tmux window in the configured webterm session, selects
that window for new webterm tabs, and keeps the window open when the resume
command exits with an error so the failure message is visible.

The connection monitor probes the configured WebTerm URL with an HTTP request.
If the URL is protected by mTLS, set `SESSION_CONTROL_MONITOR_WEBTERM_CLIENT_CERT` and
`SESSION_CONTROL_MONITOR_WEBTERM_CLIENT_KEY` to a dedicated monitor identity
accepted by the proxy. If WebTerm uses a private server CA, set
`SESSION_CONTROL_MONITOR_WEBTERM_CA_CERT` as well. The CA is added to the
system trust store for this probe; normal server certificate verification
stays enabled. The monitor allows this explicitly configured legacy CA without
a `keyUsage` extension; it still verifies the certificate chain and hostname.
The client identity is used only for the configured WebTerm
monitor target, not other HTTP targets; redirects with the certificate are
followed only when they stay on the same HTTPS origin. Keep the private key
outside git and readable only by the session-control service user. The proxy
must authorize this identity for the probed URL.

## Assistant Usage

When Codex session files include `token_count` events, the index page shows the
newest known last-turn token usage, context window, session total, plan type,
and primary/secondary rate-limit percentages.

When Claude Code session files include assistant `message.usage` objects, the
index page shows the newest known last-turn token usage, session token total,
cache token counts, model, and service tier. Claude Code local session files do
not record plan limit windows, reset times, or usage percentages, so the web UI
labels Claude limits as not locally recorded instead of inventing a limit value.

Set `SESSION_CONTROL_CLAUDE_STATUS_POLL=1` to have the web service periodically
run a sanitized Claude CLI status command. The default command is
`claude auth status --json`, which reports auth/subscription status on current
Claude Code releases but still does not expose usage-limit windows or reset
percentages. If a future Claude CLI version adds limit fields to that JSON,
session-control will surface sanitized limit/usage fields automatically.
When authenticated and the status command has no limit fields, the poller also
queries `/usage` in a fresh print-mode session with `--no-session-persistence`.
It never resumes a saved conversation, so probes do not append to chat history
or create saved sessions requiring cleanup. Unsupported or failed probes leave
limits unavailable; there is no fallback to resuming user sessions.
`SESSION_CONTROL_CLAUDE_STATUS_POLL_INTERVAL` controls the interval (default:
300 seconds). Account limits can change through activity in other sessions, so
polling does not depend on changes to any one local transcript.
When running under systemd, set `SESSION_CONTROL_CLAUDE_STATUS_COMMAND` to an
absolute `claude` path if the service PATH cannot find the CLI.

## Google AGY Multi-User Profiles & Usage Tracing

`session-control` supports isolated multi-user environments, workspace routing,
and local token usage tracing for the Google Antigravity CLI (`agy`) without
modifying protected system OAuth credentials.

Each profile is its own directory, `~/.gemini` for the default account and
`~/.gemini/profiles/<name>` for the others. `agy-profile` launches `agy` with
`--gemini_dir` pointed at that directory. `agy` does not read `GEMINI_DIR`, so
a launch without that flag stays on the account already signed in at `~/.gemini`.
The first launch of a new profile prints a Google sign-in URL. Pick the other
account on that page. A browser that is already signed in will otherwise offer
the same account again.

```bash
# View configured profiles and active token metrics
agy-profile list
session-control profile list

# Check resolved profile for current working directory
agy-profile current

# View token consumption and session breakdown
agy-profile usage
agy-profile usage --json

# Launch agy with automatic profile selection and usage harvesting
agy-profile [args...]
agy-profile run [args...]

# Add or switch profiles
agy-profile add work --email dev@example.com
agy-profile switch work

# Define directory or repository routing rules
agy-profile route add "*/research-repos/*" academic
agy-profile route list
```

Token events (`input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`) are incrementally
harvested from conversation transcripts into a local SQLite telemetry database at
`~/.gemini/usage_tracking.sqlite`.

## Grok Multi-Account Profiles

Grok accounts use the same shape. Each account is an isolated `GROK_HOME`.
The default account remains `~/.grok`. Added accounts default to
`~/.grok/profiles/<name>`, with their own `auth.json` and sessions. The
registry itself stays at `~/.grok/profiles.json`.

```bash
grok-profile list
grok-profile current
grok-profile usage
grok-profile usage --json

grok-profile add work --email work@example.com
grok-profile switch work
grok-profile route add "*/research-repos/*" academic
grok-profile route list

# First launch of a new account opens Grok's normal sign-in in that home.
grok-profile run --profile work login
grok-profile
grok-profile --resume <session-id>
```

`session-control grok-profile` accepts the same subcommands. Token totals are
read from each session's `usage.json` into `~/.grok/profile_usage.sqlite`.
Sessions from added accounts show up in the control plane, and their resume
command goes through `grok-profile run --profile <name>`.

## Codex, Claude Code, Continue, and Copilot accounts

These four CLIs already keep one login per directory. `session-control` wraps
that the same way as Grok:

| Launcher | CLI variable | Default home | Sign-in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `codex-profile` | `CODEX_HOME` | `~/.codex` | `codex-profile run --profile NAME login` |
| `claude-profile` | `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | `~/.claude` | `claude-profile run --profile NAME auth login` |
| `continue-profile` | `CONTINUE_GLOBAL_DIR` | `~/.continue` | `continue-profile run --profile NAME login` |
| `copilot-profile` | `COPILOT_HOME` | `~/.copilot` | `copilot-profile run --profile NAME login` |

Added accounts default to `<home>/profiles/<name>`. The registry stays at
`<home>/profiles.json`, and token totals go to `<home>/profile_usage.sqlite`.
`codex --profile` is a Codex config overlay, not a second ChatGPT account.
Use `codex-profile` when the login itself should change.

```bash
codex-profile add work --email work@example.com
codex-profile route add "*/clients/*" work
claude-profile list
continue-profile usage
copilot-profile current
```

`session-control codex-profile` and the other three names accept the same
subcommands. A resume from an added account goes through that account's
launcher, so the control plane opens the directory that owns the session.

The launchers remove `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`,
`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `CONTINUE_API_KEY`, `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`,
`GH_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_TOKEN` from the child process. Those variables would
otherwise override the login stored in the selected directory. Running
`codex`, `claude`, `cn`, or `copilot` directly still uses whatever the shell
already exported.

Codex totals keep the latest `total_token_usage` in each session file. Claude
Code and Copilot totals add each recorded call, including cache tokens.
Continue totals add `usage` objects when a session file has them.

## Delete Behavior

Delete actions move session files or directories into the configured trash
directory instead of hard-deleting them immediately. Continue, Codex, Grok,
and AGY indexes are updated when a session is removed. Grok's active-session
registry, AGY presence/status metadata, and Copilot's live `inuse.<pid>.lock`
prevent deletion of sessions that appear to be in use. AGY summary and search
rows—including its opaque raw summary blob—are preserved in validated restore
metadata so delete remains reversible.

Each newly deleted or pruned session records local restore metadata alongside
its trash payload. List candidates, then restore one by its exact displayed
identifier:

```bash
session-control restore --list
session-control restore 20260827T120000Z/continue/<session-id>
```

Restore only accepts an entry beneath the configured trash directory, returns
every file to its original provider-relative path, rebuilds provider indexes
when needed, and refuses to overwrite any existing target or provider index
entry. Sessions moved to trash before this feature do not have restore metadata
and remain manual recovery cases.

## Pruning

Pruning uses the same delete-to-trash path as the web UI. A session is eligible
when its last activity timestamp is older than the configured age; active
sessions are skipped.

Preview the default 180-day cleanup:

```bash
session-control prune --older-than 180d --dry-run
```

Run the cleanup:

```bash
session-control prune --older-than 180d
```

Preview and clean up only short subagents after one day of inactivity:

```bash
session-control prune --short-subagents-only --older-than 1d --dry-run
session-control prune --short-subagents-only --older-than 1d
```

The scoped command uses the same trash and restore flow. Review the dry run
before deleting; a brief subagent may still contain useful work.

To prune short subagents sooner during the regular scheduled run, use either
relative form. With a `180d` baseline, `25%` and `4x` both set a `45d` cutoff
for short subagents while other sessions keep the `180d` cutoff:

```bash
session-control prune --older-than 180d --short-subagent-percent 25% --dry-run
session-control prune --older-than 180d --short-subagent-multiplier 4x --dry-run
```

Set one matching `SESSION_CONTROL_PRUNE_SHORT_SUBAGENT_*` variable in the local
environment file to apply it to the installed daily timer. CLI flags override
the environment setting for one run. Both forms also work with
`--short-subagents-only`.

Install the daily user-level clockwork timer:

```bash
./scripts/install_prune_timer.sh --older-than 180d
```

The timer is rendered from
`config/clockwork/prune-sessions.toml.template` and runs daily at 03:35 with a
small randomized delay. It can be inspected with:

```bash
systemctl --user list-timers session-control-prune.timer
```
